newsitem.title: USA: Pilots/industry differ on crash avoidance systems.
newsitem.headline: Pilots/industry differ on crash avoidance systems.

text.p: Airlines pilots and federal safety officials differed with the cargo industry at a Congressional hearing on Wednesday over the early installation of new equipment to avoid midair collisions.
Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance Systems (TCAS) are now required by law on all passenger planes, but not on cargo craft.
The TCAS alerts a pilot with a shrill sound in the cockpit when another plane comes in close proximity, giving him direction commands to avoid a possible midair collision.
An ACAS alerted the pilot of a Nations Air Boeing 737 off New Jersey on February 5 when two Air Force F-16s closed in on it, and directed him to take sharp evasive action.
Randolph Babbitt, president of the Air Line Pilots Association, said TCAS was a proven technology and there was no reason why it should not be installed on cargo planes.
He told the House of Representatives aviation subcommittee that "The time has come to equalize the level of safety between the cargo fleet and their passenger-carrying counterparts."
Babbitt, whose union represents 46,000 pilots at 45 airlines, said these could be installed by the end of next year by legislation or Federal Aviation Administration action.

He was backed by the Independent Pilots Association, which represents 2100 pilots at United Parcel Service of America Inc., and by Robert Francis, vice chairman of the National Transportation Safety Board.
Francis said that since TCAS was first installed, FAA figures showed that reported near midair collision fell from 454 in 1990 to an all-time low of 202 in 1996.
"We believe that TCAS installation played a major role in the improvement shown," he said.
Francis said TCAS should be increasingly valuable for cargo companies who fly mostly at night and into high density hubs.
But Stephen Alterman, president of the Air Freight Association, a trade group, said that while his members backed the use of collision-avoidance systems, TCAS was outmoded.
He told the panel than other technology already being developed by the cargo industry is based on satellite detection and location equipment providing more accurate data.
Alterman said this could be certified by the FAA and installed beginning in early 1998. In addition, he said, this system could be used by small aircraft, as well.
With this, he said "the entire aviation system will benefit in terms of both safety and operations efficiencies."
